source_text: Constabit autem consequentissime mortem perpetuam, id est poenam sempiternam, ad nos non fuisse transmissam ac per hoc peccatum traducis esse non posse. Ut enim breviter, quid tenendum constet, appareat; ab Apostolo dona Christi peccato primi hominis praeferuntur; tu per hoc peccatum tuum id est traducis unam dicis an duas transisse mortes? Si unam et corporalem, ut hic confessus es, constat gratiam Christi antecellere peccato primi hominis et iam nascitur nemo peccator, quia, si ut supra dixisti, regnum peccati est, ut in secundam homo mortem id est in poenam perpetuam praecipitetur, et per Adam mortem corporis solum advectam dicis, nec peccatum per Adam ad posteros nec mors aeterna transmittitur.
pass_a_gloss: But it will stand most consequently that perpetual death, that is everlasting punishment, was not transmitted to us and through this that the sin of the tradux cannot be. For that it may appear briefly what stands to be held; by the Apostle the gifts of Christ are preferred to the sin of the first human being; do you say that through this sin of yours, that is of the tradux, one death passed or two? If one and bodily, as you have confessed here, it stands that the grace of Christ excels the sin of the first human being and already no one is born a sinner, because, if as you said above, the kingdom of sin is that a human being be hurled into a second death, that is into perpetual punishment, and you say that through Adam only the death of the body was brought on, neither sin through Adam to posterity nor eternal death is transmitted.

lemmas.lexica: LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS mors; Blaise temporal vs eternal death in Rom 5
LS Poenus=Carthaginian; Julian's slur for Augustine

pass_b_english: It will follow entirely consistently that everlasting death—that is, eternal punishment—was not transmitted to us, and consequently that sin transmitted by descent cannot exist. To make briefly clear the position we must hold: the apostle ranks Christ’s gifts above the first man’s sin. Do you say that through this sin of yours—the sin of inherited transmission—one death passed on, or two? If one, and bodily death, as you have confessed here, then Christ’s grace clearly excels the first man’s sin, and no one is born a sinner. For if, as you said above, sin’s kingdom consists in a person being hurled into the second death, or everlasting punishment, and you say that through Adam only bodily death was brought on, then neither sin nor eternal death is transmitted through Adam to his descendants (compare Romans 5:15; Revelation 20:14).

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
